Roger, a middle-aged man with a sturdy build, dark hair greying at the temples, and a weathered face etched with quiet resolve, walks across the Marktplatz Altdorf holding the small hand of Lukas, a school-age boy with light brown hair and curious eyes, dressed in a simple linen tunic. The November afternoon is cool and grey; the air carries the smell of wood smoke and wet fallen leaves scattered across the stone square. In the centre of the plaza, dominating the composition, stands a tall wooden pole planted vertically in the ground—roughly three times a man's height—with Gesslers Hut auf der Stange secured at its very top: a wide-brimmed dark wool hat with a rounded crown, tied on with a visible cord looped around the pole tip, swaying slightly in the breeze. At the base of the pole, a Soldier1—an adult of average stocky build with short dark brown hair, brown eyes, and a clean-shaven square jaw—stands alert in his dark iron chain mail hauberk worn over a dark olive padded linen gambeson, dark brown leather gauntlets, a plain iron skullcap, dark wool trousers, and heavy leather boots; his mouth is open as if calling out in proclamation to the gathered townsfolk. Lukas gazes upward at the hat on the pole, his small face turning back toward Roger with a puzzled expression as he squeezes his father's hand. Roger faces left, looking down at his son with a calm, measured expression, his posture steady and protective. The square stretches wide behind them, with anonymous market-goers in rust, brown, and grey wool cloaks and tunics visible in soft focus at the margins—a distant crowd of villagers moving slowly through the plaza, some pausing to acknowledge the pole. Medium-wide shot capturing the tension between the intimate moment of father and child and the imposing symbol of authority at the square's heart.
